runs.text: First paint after choosing a repository should land under 30 ms: open,
, root tree, refs. Everything else is on demand.
Read the header before the body.
check size from the object header; a 2 GiB blob costs a header read.
Never walk a subtree to answer a question about a folder.
pages; the UI asks for the next page when scrolled and keeps the cursor with the tip's cached pages, so returning to a tip resumes. Filtered history pages through one
per scope or search. Only a cursor that lost its place (a dropped stale page) is replaced, and the new one re-walks the pages already shown once.
Key every cache on an object id.

The text view lays out lazily; the ruler draws visible fragments from line starts precomputed with the document; syntax colors apply per visible chunk as the user scrolls. Do not build per-line views, and do not walk the whole document on the main actor.
Let the index answer for the working tree.
A status walk hashes a file only when the blob header's size matches
the index cannot vouch for it: an entry whose recorded

still matches disk, whose id is the tree's, and that is not racy means the file was not touched. Every other case reads the file, so the cache can drop a hash but never a change. Hashing every size-matched file instead costs an order of magnitude on a large checkout.
Coalesce repeated requests, never queue them.

keeps one scan in flight and at most one queued re-run, because a working tree can change faster than it can be walked. Spawning a task per filesystem event builds a backlog that never drains — it cost 190 000 suspended tasks and 638 MB once.
process costs more than any operation above.
Do not build a parallel index.
, and the multi-pack index are the index. A repository missing

to the user rather than writing it. The one sanctioned exception is path search: it flattens the selected root once, in the background, keyed by the root tree id, cancellable, and capped at 200 000 entries. Only the two most recently searched roots keep their index; the walk reads through

without storing in it, so rebuilding an evicted one reads its directories again. In the working tree it walks disk instead, once per opening of the panel, capped the same way, with ignored folders the tree does not track pruned unopened. Content search reads that same list and builds nothing of its own: each search reads the files it lists, a batch at a time.
Syntax highlighting and blame load after the content is on screen and never block it; a stale result is dropped by generation, like every other load.
Parse for a feature when the user reaches for it.

Import links need a second parse of the file, which costs about as much as highlighting it, so it runs on the first pointer move over the text. A file opened from the sidebar and read costs nothing extra.

kind.text:
cargo build --release -p rc-git-cli
target/release/rc-git --time ls   <repo>            # open + root tree
target/release/rc-git --time refs <repo>
target/release/rc-git --time cat  <repo> HEAD path/to/file
target/release/rc-git --time log  <repo> -n 100
target/release/rc-git --time changes <repo>         # the full working-tree status walk
target/release/rc-git --time files <repo>           # the working-tree walk path search uses
target/release/rc-git --time grep <repo> <text>     # content search over every blob at HEAD
target/release/rc-git --time highlight <repo> HEAD path/to/file   # one highlight pass
target/release/rc-git --time links <repo> HEAD path/to/file.ts    # one import-link pass

runs.text: reports the open and the command separately on stderr, so the two can be tracked apart. For statistics over many runs use
around the same commands. Compare against
on the same repository to keep the numbers honest.
Cold page cache: the first open of a large pack pays for disk reads; nothing to do in code.
Long delta chains: a blob at the end of a chain inflates every base. gix caches bases per handle, which is why handles are pooled instead of created per call.
